sections.h2: Selling a house in Edison, NJ
sections.html:
Edison is a Middlesex County township where a sale usually hinges on one local document, the Residential Resale Certificate, plus a state smoke certificate that has to come first. Nothing here is complicated, yet every step takes calendar time, so get going the moment a buyer signs.

The township has 109,077 residents and 38,098 households. Roughly 61 percent of homes are owner occupied, the median home value is $496,900, and median household income is $125,145. Many named sections, among them Stelton, Menlo Park, Oak Tree, Raritan Manor, Clara Barton, Lindenau and Washington Park, show up in listings, so use the right one.

sections.h2: What the Edison resale certificate requires
sections.html:
Edison Township Ordinance 14-1.6 says a Certificate for Change of Ownership must be obtained before the property closes, and the township form warns of fines up to $2,000 for skipping it. The application fee is $150, paid by certified check, credit card or money order. No cash, no personal checks and no refunds. Code Enforcement takes the application by email at the resale address printed on the form and then calls for a card payment.

Timing is the part that trips people up. Ask for the inspection at least four weeks before the closing date. A smoke certificate must already exist before the resale certificate can be issued, and the inspector wants a copy on site.

What the Edison inspector checks on a one or two family home
AreaWhat the form asks for
PermitsAdditions, finished basements or attics, garage conversions, patios, decks, pools and spas need verified permits
Pools and spasFence and childproof gate
Stairs and railsSecure guardrails and handrails; stair riser openings under 4 inches
MechanicalsWater heater with relief valve and piping ending 6 inches off the floor; tight flue connections; shut-off valves on gas appliances
DryerVented outside, not into a garage, attic or basement
OutsideHouse numbers at least 4 inches high at the front
InteriorWorking GFI outlets, no keyed locks on bedroom doors or inside egress doors, no junk or debris

• The current owner must resolve it, even if a previous owner did the work.
  • You pull a compliance permit, have the work inspected and close the permit before the certificate is issued.
  • Before the inspection, check the Building Department for open permits and ask the Tax Assessor whether improvements such as a finished basement are on the township record.
  • The ordinance covers every change of ownership, so a sale to a cash buyer still needs the certificate before closing.

An open permit is the usual reason an Edison closing slips, so request the address's permit history from the Building Department the day you list. A house that has changed hands more than once is more likely to carry a finished basement, deck or addition from an earlier owner.

Edison surrounds the borough of Metuchen and sits roughly 27 miles from both Midtown Manhattan and Trenton.

  • Rail: Edison station in South Edison runs NJ Transit Northeast Corridor trains to Newark Penn, New York Penn and Trenton, and North Edison residents may be closer to Metropark or Metuchen stations.
  • Roads: Route 27, Route 440, U.S. Route 1, Interstate 287 and about five miles of the New Jersey Turnpike, with Exit 10 inside the township.
  • Jobs: Raritan Center, a 2,300 acre business park, plus warehouse hubs and an Amazon fulfillment center.

The average commute is 33.9 minutes. Edison Township Public Schools split the township between two high schools: homes in the south feed Edison High School, and homes in the north feed J.P. Stevens High School. Name the attendance zone for your street when you list, because families filter by high school before they filter by anything else.

Rain and melted snow add up to about 49.6 inches a year, so a buyer's inspector will look closely at the roof, gutters and basement walls, and the township checklist adds the water heater and stair rails. Fixing a damp basement corner or a loose guardrail before you list costs less than negotiating it after the inspection report.

Tax appeals are filed with the Middlesex County Board of Taxation, and hearings there are in person only. The deadline is April 1, moved to May 1 where a municipality has done a revaluation. Properties assessed above $1,000,000 can go straight to the State Tax Court.

The state realty transfer fee is the seller's bill at closing, unless the deed qualifies for an exemption. For recording, New Jersey residents selling in Edison sign GIT/REP-3. Sellers living elsewhere use GIT/REP-1 or GIT/REP-2, unless they fit one of the seller's assurances.

The Middlesex County Clerk records every deed for Edison at the County Administration Building, 75 Bayard Street, New Brunswick. The office takes walk-ins on weekdays, opening at 8:30 and closing at 4:10, with a 4:00 arrival cutoff. Paper filings need a cover sheet, and skipping it adds a $20 indexing charge. The deed must say "Prepared by," list tax block, lot and consideration, and carry a return address.

Most Edison closings go through an attorney or title company that records electronically, so this matters mainly when you sell without one.

sections.h2: Order of steps for a quick Edison closing
sections.html:
Once you have a signed contract, book the smoke certificate with Fire Prevention first, since the resale certificate cannot be issued without it. Email the resale application to Code Enforcement and pay the $150 fee by the accepted methods. Ask for an inspection date at least four weeks before closing, and have the smoke certificate on hand for the inspector. Meanwhile, check the Building Department for open permits and fix guardrails, dryer venting, house numbers and any other checklist items yourself, so the visit passes the first time. Walk each room beforehand with the table above in hand and clear any junk or debris.

Selling to a cash buyer changes none of this, because the ordinance covers every change of ownership and the certificate is still due before closing. What you skip is the lender's appraisal, one fewer source of delay. Keep the certificate, the smoke certificate and the permit closeouts together, since the buyer's attorney or title company will ask for them, and tell any tenants the inspection date so someone can let the inspector in.

faqs.q: How much does the Edison resale certificate cost?
faqs.a: The township form lists a $150 fee. It must be paid by certified check, credit card or money order, with no cash, no personal checks and no refunds. Fines of up to $2,000 apply if you close without the certificate.

faqs.q: Do I need the smoke certificate before the Edison inspection?
faqs.a: Yes. The smoke certificate is required before the resale certificate can be issued. If the Fire Prevention inspection happens first, give the inspector a copy at the resale visit or email it to the township's resale address.

faqs.q: Can I sell an Edison house with a finished basement that has no permit?
faqs.a: You can sell it, but the certificate will not issue until a permit is obtained, the work passes inspection and the permit is closed. Check with the Building Department and the Tax Assessor before you schedule the inspection.

faqs.q: Which county office records an Edison deed?
faqs.a: The Middlesex County Clerk in New Brunswick. The office is open weekdays from 8:30 a.m. and requires arrival by 4:00 p.m., and paper documents need a cover sheet.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to appeal an Edison property tax assessment?
faqs.a: April 1 of the tax year, or May 1 when the township completed a revaluation. File with the Middlesex County Board of Taxation. Properties assessed above $1,000,000 can go straight to the State Tax Court.
